justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a recent price level around $403–404 for the underlying asset, likely a broad equity index such as the S&P 500 ETF (SPY) or similar instrument. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed price, adding only a small positive drift consistent with the long-run average daily return for equities. At the one-week horizon, I extrapolated that drift slightly further while acknowledging mean-reversion tendencies and the possibility of short-term consolidation. At the one-month horizon, the point estimate drifts modestly higher still, reflecting the historical positive equity risk premium over multi-week periods, but the incremental upward adjustment is deliberately conservative given elevated macro uncertainty.

The confidence interval widths reflect standard realized volatility scaling across horizons. Daily equity volatility on a broad index tends to run around 1–1.5% in normal regimes, which translates to a roughly ±3.5% band for the one-day 90% interval. As I extend to one week, volatility scales by roughly the square root of time, widening the band to approximately ±7%. At one month, the interval widens further to roughly ±13–14%, capturing the compounding uncertainty over approximately 21 trading days. I also factored in the possibility of volatility regime shifts — markets can transition from low-vol to high-vol environments quickly — which nudged the intervals slightly wider than pure historical vol scaling alone would suggest.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data (e.g., a surprise in inflation, employment, or GDP growth) that prompts aggressive central bank repricing, geopolitical escalation, or a credit or liquidity event in a systemically important institution. On the upside, unexpectedly strong earnings, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of ongoing geopolitical tensions could push prices well above the upper bounds. At the one-month horizon in particular, the range of plausible macro scenarios is wide enough that I would not be surprised to see realized outcomes outside my stated 90% interval — tail events in equity markets occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict due to the well-documented fat-tailed nature of return distributions.
